title: How Grimm's Fairy Tales Work
summary: Hosts Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant (with guest host Noel sitting in) discuss Grimm's Fairy Tales as the second part of a two-parter, following the earlier episode on the Juniper Tree and Brothers Grimm. Topics include the definition of fairy tales versus fables and nursery rhymes, oral versus literary fairy tales, the Little Red Riding Hood origin study by Jamie Tehrani, the Grimm brothers' lives, German romanticism, their misleading preface and sources, how the collection was sanitized over seven editions, violent tales like The Juniper Tree and How Children Played Butcher, evil stepmother motifs, interpretations (sociohistorical, Freudian, Jack Zipes), feminist rewrites, Nazi co-option and anti-Semitic tales, and children's literature trends. The episode closes with listener mail about vocal fry.

segments.title: Opening banter and the nature of fairy tales
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the two-part fairy tale episode, share reactions, and discuss how fairy tales lack character development, are anonymous and minimalist, and how they are hard to define compared with fables, nursery rhymes, and folklore.

segments.title: Oral versus literary fairy tales and Little Red Riding Hood's origins
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish oral tales, often passed down by women during domestic work, from literary tales by Charles Perrault and Hans Christian Andersen. They describe a 2009 study by Jamie Tehrani applying biological phylogenetic methods to Little Red Riding Hood, tracing it back to roughly the sixth century BC and grouping variants worldwide.

segments.title: Early lives of the Brothers Grimm and German romanticism
segments.summary: Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm's upbringing, their father's death when they were ten, their law school education, and their work as philologists and linguists in the context of German romanticism and fears that oral folk culture was disappearing due to industrialization.

segments.title: Original collection and misleading preface
segments.summary: The original collection, Nursery and Household Tales, had 86 stories. The brothers claimed their tales were pure German peasant lore from sources like Dorothea Viehmann, but she was a French-descended tailor's wife from the merchant class, and they relied on many other written sources, misrepresenting their origins in the preface.

segments.title: Working relationship, dictionary, and editions of the collection
segments.summary: The brothers worked closely together as librarians and philologists; Jacob stayed single while Wilhelm married and had children. They started a German dictionary that was unfinished at their deaths. The fairy tale book went through seven editions, and it was sanitized for children after poor early sales, removing sexual content and the preface lies.

segments.title: Violence, stepmothers, and The Juniper Tree
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the persistence of violence in the tales and the replacement of real parents with evil stepmothers, linked to historical realities of childbirth deaths and remarriage. They summarize The Juniper Tree, in which a stepmother kills her stepson, serves him in a stew, and he is reborn as a bird.

segments.title: How Children Played Butcher story
segments.summary: The hosts read and discuss the short Grimm tale How Children Played Butcher, in which a child kills his brother while playing butcher, the mother kills the other child and then herself, and the father dies of grief, with the hosts comparing it to dark, morally blunt tales.

segments.title: Interpretations of fairy tales and Cinderella type stories
segments.summary: The hosts cover the role of fairy tales as lessons on danger and strangers, Tatar's view that the violence resembles Tom and Jerry cartoons, Jack Zipes's view of comeuppance and tyrants, Cinderella tale classifications, and interpretive approaches including sociohistorical, Freudian (Bruno Bettelheim), and Jungian readings.

segments.title: Rewrites, Nazi co-option, and anti-Semitism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss feminist rewrites of fairy tales, the film Freeway as a reworked Little Red Riding Hood, the Nazis' use of Grimm tales in schools, the Allied ban afterward, and the anti-Semitic tale The Jew in the Brambles.

segments.title: Sign-off and promotional mentions
segments.summary: The hosts mention the children's literature shift away from Grimm tales toward realism and then fantasy, then close with show contact information and where to find more.
